title: Eindhoven band and the Gestapo search on the train to Denmark
summary: He led a band in Eindhoven, then on the way to meet Bobby in Denmark, Gestapo on the train seized Glyn Paque's dice and record player.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Speaking about Harlem, in ...(?)... When Bobby left... You see, Linkback(?) and I got together somehow or other. We played up in Helleman(?), Einholden.... Oh, we were supposed to meet Bobby in 1938 at the National Scala in Denmark. Last time, you know, the doctor was here from Holland, they brought a band over in Holland for Duke Ellington's memorial or something...

He was my trumpet player. He said, "I know you. I was your trumpet player." They have like a county fair, sponsored I think by Norelco -- their factory is in Einholden. Helleman(?) is close to it. Well, the band was in my name with Alpha(?) Pay(?). We had a boy called Sondheim(?) on drums, Glyn Paque, myself, and we did...we played there, I remember, in Einholden and Helleman(?)...

Now, from there we were supposed to meet Bobby. That means we had to take a train, to go through Germany all up to Denmark. We had to pass a good deal of time. So in the inside... I remember Glyn Paque had this thing and had magazines from home. At that time there was...called Ken(?) Magazine, and Ken(?) Magazine had a headline, "Nazis Try To Kidnap Joe Louis." And we have this magazine. So I said, "Look, we're going through Germany, man. You'd better get..." -- you know. He says, "Aw..." So, sure enough, people would start coming into the train, you know, and it's a holiday crowd, and these German people are coming in to go to different places -- start jammin' in. I didn't know...

But apparently... Then the Gestapo comes in. "Where are you going?" They wanted to know where we were going, and I told them... You know, I turned the magazines around. They looked at the magazine. Evidently, they didn't know
any English, because they didn't say anything! But they demanded our passports and all that.

Then the people started coming in, see. Now, that wasn't so bad. So we had to give up our...you know, we had to give them when they'd come into the seats...you know, you had to... You know how the trains are built over there. We got crowded and everything. And ...(?)..., an old man, a family man, looked at us and says, "You're Americans, I suppose." There was a lot of misunderstanding about us. He said, "Yeah..." He went along with us. He was a nice... We didn't talk about too much. And the kids liked us. The train was becoming very crowded.

And then later on, getting near the border to Denmark, you know, it got scarce. And that's the time, boy! -- they struck on us. The Gestapo came in and they confiscated a pair of dice that we had and all that, you know.
Yeah. Glyn had dice. And the cards and the... You know those little windup... In those days you had to wind up your little record player, you know. They took that. They held us up at the border.
What grounds did they take that on? Why did they...?
They wanted to know... Well, when they caught the dice they said we were gambling on the train, etcetera,
you know. So we eventually convinced them that we were musicians and not (?). They gave us a hard time, but eventually they let us go.
